title: The Argument for Earnest and Amicable Argument
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. makes the case that argument is a precious inheritance of democratic civilization, the basis of critical reading, logical writing, deep listening, and problem solving. He rejects the zero-sum showdown model and draws on Richard Fulkerson and others to define argument as cooperative deliberation where the goal is a good decision and every participant risks having to change their mind. After trying labels like Fulkersonian and collegial, he settles on earnest and amicable, serious and joyful at once. His justification is long-term flourishing: he imagines family dinners, presidential debates, and social media if people were fluent in collaborative argument. He concedes students need not become competitive debaters, but wants every child competent at cordial, evidence-based disagreement. The piece is an excerpt of a chapter from his book These 6 Things.
points: Argument is reframed as cooperative truth-seeking whose goal is a good decision, not victory, which changes what a teacher builds in class culture.
The chosen term earnest and amicable pairs sincere conviction with friendship, so the culture is both serious and joyful.
The justification is long-term flourishing: collaborative argument skills serve students at home, in communities, and in civic life, not only in school.
Stuart does not require every student to become a technical debater; the target is lasting competence in cordial, evidence-based disagreement.
quotes: Something that is precious (from the Latin pretium, or price) is highly valuable; it is to be treated with the greatest of care.

The ability to argue makes one able to read critically, to write logically and compellingly, to listen at a level beyond compliance, and to carry on complex conversations aimed at solving problems or settling disputes.
The only way this can make sense is if we conceive of argument as something broader and deeper than a zero-sum showdown.
Earnest and amicable arguments are both serious and joyful, good for the mind and good for the soul. That’s what I’m after in my classroom.
This is the argumentative culture — or, more accurately, counter-culture — that I’m trying to create in my classroom.
How different would televised presidential debates be if getting to the bottom of things cooperatively was the norm? Or the social media chatter around those debates?

I can be content if my children don’t grow up to be competitive debaters; I will feel that I’ve failed, however, if they lack lots of practice and competence with collaborative, cordial argument by the time they leave my house.
